paper_context.research_question: Can a new, corpus-derived linear formula using Vietnamese-specific surface features (sentence length in characters, word length in characters, and percentage of difficult words from an 'easy' list) accurately predict Vietnamese text readability categories?
main_claims: A new corpus of ~1,000 Vietnamese documents (categorized into Easy/Normal/Difficult by experts) was built and is sufficiently reliable for readability research (Fleiss' kappa = 0.422).

A linear readability formula Readability = 0.004*ASLC + 0.1905*AWLC + 2.7147*PDW2 − 0.7295 (ASLC = avg sentence length in characters, AWLC = avg word length in characters, PDW2 = percent of difficult words based on an 'easy' list) predicts expert-assigned readability categories with ~81% overall accuracy (fold-averaged).
Features derived from an 'easy' frequent-word list extracted from the corpus (PDW2) correlate better with readability in this dataset than external frequency lists (PDW1/PDS1 from Dien & Hao).
Traditional surface features (sentence length, word length, percent difficult words) remain useful predictors for Vietnamese readability.
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Corpus quality: size, source diversity, annotation protocol, inter-annotator agreement (Fleiss' kappa = 0.422) and potential label noise from excluded ambiguous items.
Predictive validity: cross-validated accuracy per class (Easy/Normal/Difficult), confusion patterns, and robustness across folds.
Model selection and statistical soundness: feature selection procedure (correlation thresholding), multicollinearity handling, regression diagnostics, and whether linear model assumptions hold.
Generalizability: performance on out-of-domain texts, different registers, and on finer-grained difficulty levels not present in the three-category setup.
Comparative baseline: performance versus prior Vietnamese formulas (Nguyen & Henkin) and adapted English formulas (e.g., Flesch, Dale-Chall) when applied to the same corpus.
Reproducibility and resource sharing: availability of the corpus, frequency lists (PDW2), preprocessing details (tokenization, syllable counting), and code to reproduce experiments.
Interpretability and practical utility: ease of computing features, interpretability of coefficients, and applicability to real-world tasks (education, publishing).

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript constructs a ~1,000-document Vietnamese readability corpus labeled Easy/Normal/Difficult by experts, engineers a set of Vietnamese-specific surface features (sentence/word length measured in characters/syllables and percent difficult words from two frequency lists), and derives a simple linear formula by sequential correlation-based feature selection and 5-fold cross-validated linear regression. The paper's main logical chain: build corpus -> extract features -> select features by high correlation and remove highly mutual correlated ones -> fit linear regression across folds -> round predictions to nearest class -> report ~81% overall accuracy and per-class rates. The argument is coherent at a high level but several methodological and inferential steps are under-specified and create risks of circularity (PDW2 derived from Easy subset of same corpus), omitted uncertainty quantification (no SE/CIs for coefficients, kappa, or accuracies), and possible leakage across cross-validation folds. The reported correlations and fold accuracies support the claim that surface features can predict annotator-assigned readability within this corpus, but generalizability and statistical stability are not demonstrated. I flag specific places where the reasoning is strong (correlation patterns, monotonically varying corpus statistics) and where it breaks (feature-construction transparency, PDW2 derivation/usage, fold-level procedure details, lack of diagnostics for linear modeling and rounding-to-class decision).

Edge B->C: Collected documents labeled by experts to produce ground truth.

Edge B->D: Features computed from corpus texts.
Node E: Frequency lists — PDW1/PDS1 (Dien & Hao), PDW2/PDS2 (derived from Easy subset of corpus).
Edge D->E: Two sources for 'easy' lists compared.
Node F: Exploratory correlation analysis — Table 2 showing high pairwise correlations between TR and ASLC/AWLC/ASLS/AWLS/PDW2; low correlation for PDW1/PDS1.
Edge D+E->F: Feature correlations evaluated to inform selection.
Node G: Feature selection heuristic — rank by correlation with TR, remove features with mutual correlation >= 0.9, select ASLC, AWLC, PDW2.
Edge F->G: Correlation results drive heuristic selection.
Node H: Modeling — multiple linear regression per fold (5-fold CV), averaging coefficient values across folds to produce final formula (Eq.16).

strengths.description: Feature engineering accounts for Vietnamese orthographic and syllabic properties (characters, syllables, spaces) and evaluates both word- and syllable-level frequency lists.
evidence: Section 3.2 defines ASLS/ASLC/AWLS/AWLC and explains Vietnamese syllable/token examples.

concerns.title: Potential leakage via PDW2 construction
concerns.description: PDW2 is built from the 'Easy' subset of the same corpus used to train/test the model. If this list was computed once on the full corpus and then used across CV folds, PDW2 may encode label-derived signals and inflate correlations and predictive accuracy.
evidence: Section 3.2: 'the second is 1,000 frequent words extracted from all easy documents of our built corpus.'
Shared analysis notes risk: 'If PDW2 is derived from Easy subset or reflects dataset idiosyncrasies, predictor may exploit label-derived features (leakage)'.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Recompute PDW2 within each training split (derive frequent-word list only from training documents in each fold) and re-run CV; report accuracy change and per-fold PDW2 differences. Explicitly document PDW2 creation steps (preprocessing, thresholds) in code or supplement.

concerns.title: Under-specified preprocessing and tokenization
concerns.description: Tokenization, syllable counting, diacritic normalization, and treatment of punctuation/whitespace are described qualitatively but not specified algorithmically; these choices materially affect ASLC/AWLC/PDW measures.
evidence: Section 3.2 provides examples but lacks algorithmic detail or code pointers.

concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide exact preprocessing steps and code (or pseudo-code): normalization of diacritics, tokenization rules to split words/syllables, punctuation handling, lowercasing, and any filtering applied before frequency counting.

concerns.title: Lack of statistical uncertainty and diagnostic reporting
concerns.description: No standard errors, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported for Fleiss' kappa, correlations, regression coefficients, or accuracy estimates; no residual analysis or VIFs reported for the linear model.
evidence: Reported Fleiss' kappa = 0.422 without CIs; Table 2 lists correlations without p-values; Table 3 lists coefficients with no error bars.

concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report SEs/CIs for coefficients (per-fold and averaged), p-values or bootstrapped CIs for correlations and accuracies, VIFs for predictors, and residual diagnostics (plots or statistics) to validate linear model assumptions.

concerns.title: Evaluation decision rule (rounding) not justified
concerns.description: Rounding continuous regression outputs to nearest integer classes is an ad-hoc mapping for an ordinal outcome; alternative approaches (ordinal regression, threshold tuning) could alter classification performance and interpretation.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript presents an empirical contribution: a new Vietnamese readability corpus (~996 documents) labeled by experts into three classes (Easy/Normal/Difficult) and a simple linear readability formula derived from corpus surface features (ASLC, AWLC, PDW2). The authors used correlation-guided sequential feature selection with a 0.9 pairwise-correlation exclusion rule, trained linear regression in 5-fold cross-validation, averaged fold coefficients to produce a final formula, and mapped predicted continuous scores to discrete classes by rounding. They report fold-averaged overall accuracy ≈81% and class-wise accuracies (Easy ~76.6%, Normal ~85.7%, Difficult ~78.5%). Key methodological assumptions include validity of expert labels as ground truth, correctness and consistency of Vietnamese tokenization/syllable/character counts, absence of label leakage when deriving PDW2 (frequent words from Easy subset), and adequacy of linear regression for ordinal classification. Several procedural details needed for reproducibility and validity are missing: per-document rater assignments, fold construction/stratification rules, preprocessing/tokenization code and precise PDW2 construction steps, statistical uncertainty estimates (SEs, CIs) for kappa/correlations/coefficients/accuracies, multicollinearity diagnostics (e.g., VIFs), confusion matrices, and tests for model form (nonlinearity, interactions). The most consequential risk to the claimed predictive validity is potential leakage/circularity from deriving the PDW2 'easy' list from Easy documents of the same corpus used in training/testing. If PDW2 is built using all Easy docs before cross-validation, predictive power may be inflated and not generalize to external corpora. Other important concerns are underspecified feature extraction details (Vietnamese-specific tokenization and syllabification) and the choice to round continuous regression outputs rather than use ordinal regression or direct classification. Strengths include assembling a substantially larger Vietnamese readability corpus than previously available and reporting a compact, interpretable formula with clear feature definitions. To make the claims robust, the authors must provide reproducible preprocessing code, reconstruct PDW2 per training fold (or test on external data), report uncertainty measures, and run alternative modeling/ablation to justify modeling choices.
logical_argument_graph: Collect ~1000 documents from varied sources -> select 996 by filtering documents with 3-way rater disagreement
Ask 10 experts; each document rated by 3 experts -> assign label 1/2/3 using majority rules -> compute Fleiss' kappa = 0.422 -> claim moderate agreement and corpus reliability
Compute surface features (ASLC, AWLC, ASLS, AWLS, PDW1/2, PDS1/2) for each document using preprocessing (tokenization/syllable counting) -> produce Table 1 stats per class
Compute pairwise correlations between features and with readability (Table 2) -> identify highly correlated predictors (ASLS/ASLC/AWLS/AWLC/PDW2)
Apply sequential feature selection by correlation ranking and excluding features with mutual correlation >=0.9 -> select ASLC, AWLC, PDW2
Train OLS linear regression (Readability numeric 1/2/3) with 5-fold CV, average fold coefficients -> final formula Readability = 0.004*ASLC + 0.1905*AWLC + 2.7147*PDW2 - 0.7295
Predict continuous outputs on held-out folds, round to nearest integer to map to classes -> report per-fold/class accuracies and average overall ~81% -> claim formula predicts readability accurately

Compare PDW2 (corpus-derived) to PDW1 (external list) via correlations and modeling -> observe PDW2 much more correlated with readability and included in final formula -> claim corpus-derived list better captures 'easy' vocabulary

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript constructs a mid-scale Vietnamese readability corpus (996 documents) labeled by experts into three coarse difficulty categories. It operationalizes simple, language-aware surface features (sentence length in characters, word length in characters, and percent difficult words from a frequent-word list). Correlation analysis guided a sequential, correlation-threshold feature selection (threshold 0.9), yielding ASLC, AWLC, and PDW2. A multiple linear regression fitted by 5-fold cross-validation produced fold-wise coefficients that were averaged into a final linear formula. Predictions are continuous numeric readability values rounded to the nearest integer to obtain class labels; accuracy across folds is reported (~81% overall). The paper emphasizes that (a) corpus-derived frequent-word lists (PDW2) correlate strongly with readability in this dataset versus an external frequency list (PDW1), and (b) traditional surface metrics remain effective for Vietnamese readability. The reasoning chain depends on the corpus quality (annotation protocol and representativeness), the fidelity of feature extraction for Vietnamese orthography, the legitimacy of deriving PDW2 from the corpus (risking circularity), and the statistical adequacy of correlation-based selection plus ordinary least squares for an ordinal outcome.
logical_argument_graph: Collect diverse Vietnamese texts and assign expert readability labels (1/2/3) → obtain corpus of 996 documents with moderate inter-annotator agreement (kappa=0.422).
Define surface features adapted to Vietnamese (ASLC, AWLC, ASLS, AWLS, PDW/PDS variants).
Compute pairwise correlations between features and with readability label (Table 2).
Select features by highest correlation with readability, removing features with mutual correlation >= 0.9 → choose ASLC, AWLC, PDW2.
Fit multiple linear regression per CV fold using chosen predictors; average coefficients across 5 folds to produce final formula (Equation 16).
Predict continuous readability scores on held-out folds, round to nearest integer, compare with expert labels → report per-class and overall accuracies (~81% overall).
Interpret high PDW2 correlation as evidence corpus-derived easy-word lists are better than external lists (PDW1) for this dataset.
Conclude that simple surface features remain useful for Vietnamese readability and propose future work adding deeper linguistic features and more corpora.

concerns.title: Evaluation mapping (rounding) and absence of confusion matrices/statistical tests

prior_stage_inputs: Manuscript context (paper text, tables, refs) and Table 1-3, Equation 16
specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper constructs a ~1,000-document Vietnamese corpus labeled Easy/Normal/Difficult by experts (3 raters per doc, Fleiss' kappa=0.422), extracts simple surface features tailored to Vietnamese (sentence length in characters ASLC, word length in characters AWLC, and percent difficult words PDW2 from an 'easy' list derived from corpus Easy subset), and uses a correlation-driven feature selection (remove features pairwise-correlated >=0.9) to pick ASLC, AWLC, PDW2. A 5-fold cross-validated ordinary linear regression maps these features to numeric labels (1/2/3); coefficients are averaged across folds to produce Readability = 0.004*ASLC + 0.1905*AWLC + 2.7147*PDW2 − 0.7295. Continuous predictions are rounded to nearest integer and compared to expert labels yielding an average accuracy ≈81%. The authors argue (1) corpus is a useful resource, (2) traditional surface features remain predictive for Vietnamese, and (3) a corpus-derived easy-word list (PDW2) outperforms an external frequency list (PDW1). The manuscript's reasoning chain: collect documents → expert-label with simple majority rules → compute Vietnamese-aware surface features → assess pairwise correlations → select nonredundant features by high-correlation threshold → fit linear regressions per CV fold → average coefficients → round predictions to discrete classes → report accuracies and claim practical utility. Key inferences depend on (a) reliability of labels given moderate kappa, (b) correctness and reproducibility of Vietnamese tokenization/syllable/character counting, and (c) absence of leakage from building PDW2 on the same corpus (possible circularity).
logical_argument_graph: 1. Large, diverse document collection (~1000) -> enables more robust Vietnamese readability work than prior small corpora (Nguyen & Henkin).
2. Expert annotation protocol (3-of-3 majority; remove 3-way ties) -> yields labeled corpus (996 docs) with Fleiss' kappa = 0.422 -> claimed moderate reliability.
3. Define Vietnamese-specific surface features (ASLC, AWLC, PDW*) -> tailored feature extraction that respects orthography/syllable structure.
4. Compute feature ↔ readability correlations -> identify ASLC, AWLC, PDW2 as highly correlated with readability (Table 2).
5. Sequential feature selection removing features pairwise-correlated >=0.9 -> select ASLC, AWLC, PDW2 to mitigate redundancy.
6. Fit linear regression in 5-fold CV and average coefficients -> produce final linear formula (Equation 16).
7. Round continuous predictions to nearest integer -> yield discrete class predictions and compute accuracy (~81%).
8. Observe PDW2 (corpus-derived easy list) correlates/works better than external PDW1 -> conclude corpus-derived frequency lists better capture Vietnamese 'easy' vocabulary in this setup.
9. Conclude surface features remain useful and propose future deeper features and more datasets for improved generalizability.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper reports (a) construction of a 996-document Vietnamese readability corpus labeled Easy/Normal/Difficult by expert raters (3 ratings per document; Fleiss' kappa = 0.422), (b) definition of Vietnamese-aware surface features (sentence length in characters/syllables/words, word length in characters/syllables, and percent difficult words/syllables using two frequency lists), (c) correlation-guided sequential feature selection (exclude features pairwise-correlated ≥ 0.9) producing three predictors (ASLC, AWLC, PDW2), and (d) a 5-fold cross-validated ordinary least squares regression whose averaged coefficients yield a simple linear formula Readability = 0.004*ASLC + 0.1905*AWLC + 2.7147*PDW2 − 0.7295. Predictions were rounded to the nearest integer to obtain discrete labels and reported fold-averaged overall accuracy ≈81% (class-wise averages: Easy 76.6%, Normal 85.7%, Difficult 78.5%). Evidence in the manuscript (tables and text) supports these descriptive steps and reported numbers. Major uncertainties arise from underspecified preprocessing (tokenization, syllable counting, diacritics), lack of statistical uncertainty (SEs, CIs) for key estimates (kappa, correlations, coefficients, accuracies), and risk of circularity/leakage because PDW2 (the corpus-derived 'easy' frequent-word list) appears to be built from Easy documents that may include test fold items unless constructed per CV fold. These uncertainties materially affect claims about predictive validity and generalizability. The conclusion that simple surface features remain useful within this corpus is supported; the stronger claim that PDW2 outperforms external lists and that the formula will generalize to applied settings is only partially supported given potential leakage and absent external evaluation.
logical_argument_graph: Collect ~1,000 documents from varied sources → apply expert labeling with 3-rater per document protocol → filter out 3-way disagreements → obtain final corpus of 996 docs with class counts (Table 1).

Compute Vietnamese-aware surface features (ASLW/ASLS/ASLC, AWLS/AWLC, PDW1/PDW2/PDS1/PDS2) using word/syllable/character counts and two frequent-word/syllable lists (external Dien & Hao and corpus-derived Easy list).

Compute pairwise correlations between each feature and target readability label (TR) and among features (Table 2) → rank features by correlation with TR → sequentially select features while excluding features with pairwise correlation ≥ 0.9 → selected ASLC, AWLC, PDW2.

Train OLS regression on 4/5 folds, predict remaining fold; repeat for 5 folds → average coefficients across folds to form final linear formula (Equation 16) → round continuous outputs to nearest integer → compute fold-wise accuracies and average overall accuracy ≈81% (Table 3).
Interpret results: surface features still predictive; corpus-derived PDW2 yields higher correlation with TR than external PDW1; claim practical applicability and propose future work.

strengths.title: Substantially larger Vietnamese readability corpus
strengths.description: The authors assembled and annotated nearly one thousand Vietnamese documents categorized into three readability levels, substantially enlarging resources compared to prior Vietnamese studies (20 and 54 documents).
evidence: Manuscript Table 1 shows 996 documents; related works note prior corpora had 20 and 54 documents.

strengths.title: Language-aware, interpretable feature set
strengths.description: Features are defined with Vietnamese orthography in mind (character- and syllable-based counts, explicit percent-difficult measures), producing an interpretable and computationally simple formula.
evidence: Equations 8–14; textual examples of Vietnamese syllables and whitespace assumptions; final formula coefficients (Equation 16).

strengths.title: Transparent, compact final model
strengths.description: A simple linear formula with three predictors is clearly reported with per-fold coefficients and fold-wise accuracies, facilitating interpretability and potential practical use.
evidence: Equation 16; Table 3 listing fold-wise coefficients and accuracies; description of 5-fold CV procedure.

concerns.title: Potential leakage/circularity from PDW2 construction
concerns.description: PDW2 (the corpus-derived 'easy' frequent-word list) was built from the corpus's Easy documents; if PDW2 was constructed once using the full corpus before cross-validation, features may leak label-derived information into predictors and inflate correlations and accuracy.
evidence: Section 3.2: 'second is 1,000 frequent words extracted from all easy documents of our built corpus.'
Chaining notes and prior reviewers flagged absence of per-fold PDW2 derivation.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Recompute PDW2 inside each training fold (derive frequent-word list using only training data) and re-run CV; alternatively evaluate model on an external held-out dataset not used to build PDW2 and report differences.

concerns.title: Underspecified preprocessing and tokenization
concerns.description: Key preprocessing steps that determine ASLC/AWLC/PDW2 values (tokenization, syllable counting, diacritic normalization, punctuation handling) are described verbally but lack algorithmic detail or code, harming reproducibility and possibly altering feature values substantially.
evidence: 3.2 contains informal examples of Vietnamese syllables but no algorithmic rules or code; shared analysis notes missing preprocessing specifics.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide precise preprocessing algorithm (tokenizer used, rules for syllable segmentation, diacritic normalization), share scripts or an anonymized sample of processed documents, and show that feature computations are robust under plausible implementation choices.

concerns.title: Absence of uncertainty quantification
concerns.description: No standard errors, confidence intervals, or hypothesis tests are reported for Fleiss' kappa, correlations, regression coefficients, or accuracy estimates; this prevents assessment of estimate stability and statistical significance.
evidence: Kappa reported as 0.422 without CI; Table 2 correlations and Table 3 coefficients/accuracies reported without SEs or CIs.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report 95% CIs or SEs for kappa (e.g., bootstrap), correlation p-values, coefficient SEs (from regression), fold-wise variance of coefficients, and confidence intervals for accuracy (e.g., via bootstrap or binomial CI).

concerns.title: Feature selection and multicollinearity diagnostics underdocumented
concerns.description: Sequential correlation-thresholding used a 0.9 cutoff chosen 'through some experiments' but lacks ablation/justification; multicollinearity beyond pairwise correlations (e.g., VIFs) not reported, and averaging coefficients across folds may hide instability.
evidence: Section 3.3 describes threshold 0.9 without detailed results of experiments; Table 2 shows high mutual correlations among several features.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide ablation studies with alternative thresholds, report VIFs for chosen predictors, show coefficient variability across folds with SEs, and consider regularization (ridge) or dimensionality reduction to assess stability.

concerns.title: Evaluation mapping: rounding continuous outputs to discrete classes
concerns.description: Converting continuous regression outputs to discrete labels by simple rounding is a modeling decision that is not justified or compared to alternatives (ordinal regression, multiclass logistic, calibrated thresholds); rounding may misclassify borderline items and bias class-wise metrics.
evidence: Section 3.3: 'The predicted values were rounded to the nearest unit and compared to the expert evaluated readability for accuracy assessment.'
No comparisons to ordinal or classification baselines are provided.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Compare rounding to ordinal regression (proportional odds), multiclass logistic, or calibrated thresholding; report confusion matrices, per-class precision/recall, and metrics for ties/near-boundary cases.

concerns.title: Generalizability not demonstrated
concerns.description: Claims about practical applicability are not supported by testing on out-of-domain texts or held-out external datasets; domain composition of corpus sources is not reported so domain bias may exist.
evidence: Discussion asserts applicability; corpus sources are summarized by type (textbooks, newspapers, specialized docs) but distributions not enumerated.
No external evaluation reported.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide source breakdown, perform domain-stratified CV, and evaluate formula on external corpora or a held-out set collected from different sources/registers to measure generalization.

comparable_works.relevance: Prior Vietnamese readability formulas; small-sample baselines
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Both prior works used small corpora and surface features (word length, sentence length); this paper offers a much larger corpus and a new formula adapted to Vietnamese specifics.
comparable_works.source_trace: Manuscript references and related works section

comparable_works.relevance: Canonical readability formulas in English that motivate feature choices (sentence length, percent difficult words, syllables per word).
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similar high-level approach (surface features, linear formulas) but language-specific feature definitions differ; authors adapt the percent-difficult-word idea using Vietnamese lists.

comparable_works.relevance: Source of the external frequency lists (PDW1/PDS1) used for comparison
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: External frequency list derived from mostly newspaper corpora; authors find low correlation with readability in their corpus compared to PDW2.

uncertainty_flags: PDW2 derivation may involve leakage if created before cross-validation; need per-fold PDW2 recomputation or held-out external test.
Preprocessing/tokenization and syllable counting procedures are underspecified and affect core predictors.
No confidence intervals, SEs, or statistical tests reported for kappa, correlations, coefficients, or accuracies.
Cross-validation fold construction (stratification by class/domain) is not described; performance estimates may be optimistic if folds are not independent.
Averaging coefficients across folds without variance reporting may obscure instability; fold-wise coefficient spread appears nontrivial for AWLC and PDW2.
alternative_interpretations: High PDW2 correlation with readability could reflect dataset idiosyncrasies or leakage rather than an objectively better 'easy' list; if PDW2 was built on documents that are strongly associated with Easy labels (and included test documents), PDW2 may encode label signals.

The strong predictive power of surface features may be specific to coarse 3-class labels and the selected source mix; finer-grained or reader-centered readability tasks might require deeper linguistic features.
Moderate inter-annotator agreement (kappa=0.422) suggests label noise; reported accuracy could be partly predicting annotator consensus patterns rather than underlying reader difficulty.
transparency_notes: Authors should provide exact preprocessing code (tokenization, syllabification rules, normalization) and the scripts used to build PDW2 to enable reproduction.
Provide per-document rater assignments (which three experts rated each document) so Fleiss' kappa can be recomputed and disagreements analyzed.
Supply fold assignment information and whether PDW2 was recomputed per training fold; if not, recompute and report revised CV results.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: Although deriving a corpus-specific frequent-word list (PDW2) for Vietnamese readability and combining character-based counts is a relatively novel, language-aware engineering choice, novelty does not guarantee external validity—particularly if PDW2 construction introduces dataset-specific signals or leakage.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If PDW2 is derived strictly from training data (no test fold leakage) and model re-evaluation on external held-out data maintains similar accuracy, then the corpus-derived list is a genuine innovation improving Vietnamese readability prediction.
If preprocessing/tokenization choices are standardized and shared (with code), feature values will be reproducible and coefficients meaningful across implementations.

If ordinal modeling or alternative classification methods yield similar or better performance, the linear formula's simplicity will be credibly justified; otherwise, nonlinearity could show the linear model underfits.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The corpus is substantially larger than prior Vietnamese datasets (20/54 docs), which is a clear incremental contribution enabling empirical study. The linguistic tailoring of features to Vietnamese (character and syllable measures) is appropriate and practical.
evidence: Manuscript: Table 1 shows 996 documents; related works cite much smaller prior corpora.
uncertainty_flags: External validity and reproducibility hinge on preprocessing details and PDW2 derivation procedure.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Deriving an 'easy' frequent-word list from a corpus subset (PDW2) to compute percent-difficult and incorporating character-based sentence length are useful language-specific adjustments. However, methodological novelty risks circularity if list construction uses information from test items.
evidence: High PDW2 correlation reported (0.786) and PDW2 included in final model; PDW2 described as extracted from all Easy documents of built corpus.
uncertainty_flags: No per-fold PDW2 construction reported; authors need to demonstrate PDW2 is train-only to avoid leakage.

novelty_lenses.verdict: potentially useful within-corpus but unproven externally
novelty_lenses.rationale: The simple formula is interpretable and easy to compute, suiting educational/publishing applications, provided it generalizes to target domains and is robust to preprocessing variants.
evidence: Final formula with small number of features and reported 81% accuracy suggests practical viability.
uncertainty_flags: Generalizability and robustness not demonstrated; moderate kappa suggests label noise that may limit deployment without further validation.

confidence_interval.rationale: I am moderately confident that the manuscript's reported descriptive results (correlations, fold accuracies under their procedure) are accurate reflections of their experiments as described (hence lower bound not near 0). However, due to major methodological uncertainties—chiefly possible PDW2 leakage, underspecified preprocessing, and absence of uncertainty quantification—the true external validity and stability of the reported ~81% accuracy are substantially uncertain, so upper confidence is capped well below 1.0.

consensus_findings: A substantially larger Vietnamese readability corpus (≈996 documents) was constructed and annotated into three coarse difficulty categories (Easy/Normal/Difficult); this is a meaningful resource compared to prior Vietnamese studies.

Simple, language-aware surface features (sentence length in characters, word length in characters, percent difficult words) were defined and shown to correlate with expert-assigned readability within the presented corpus.

The manuscript derives an explicit, interpretable linear formula (coefficients for ASLC, AWLC, PDW2 and intercept) and reports approximately 81% average in-corpus accuracy under the authors' 5-fold CV + rounding evaluation procedure.

Multiple reviewers identify the same methodological and reporting gaps that materially affect confidence in predictive validity and generalizability: (1) potential circularity/leakage from constructing PDW2 from the corpus's Easy subset, (2) underspecified preprocessing/tokenization and syllable-counting steps, (3) missing uncertainty quantification (SEs/CIs) for kappa, correlations, coefficients, and accuracies, and (4) insufficient detail about CV fold construction (stratification, independence by source).
disagreements: Degree-of-concern about the reported Fleiss' kappa (0.422): some reviewers view it as 'moderate but acceptable' given task difficulty and corpus scale, while others see it as evidence of substantial label noise that requires deeper rater analysis before trusting predictive performance.

Novelty characterization: some reviewers treat the work primarily as an incremental adaptation of classic surface-based readability formulas to Vietnamese (novelty mainly in scale and resource), whereas others view the corpus-derived PDW2 and the larger corpus as a stronger innovation signal—contingent on resolving methodological safeguards (especially leakage).

Severity assigned to generalizability risks varies: a subset of reviewers rates lack of external validation as a 'major' limitation that undermines practical claims, while others view it as an important but resolvable next step that does not negate in-corpus findings.
uncertainty_hotspots: PDW2 construction and circularity: it is unclear whether PDW2 (the 1,000-word 'easy' list) was built once from the entire Easy subset prior to CV or recomputed per training fold. If constructed globally, PDW2 may leak label information and inflate correlations/accuracy.

Preprocessing/tokenization/syllabification: algorithmic details (tokenizer used, diacritic/normalization choices, punctuation handling, syllable vs word segmentation) are underspecified, but these choices directly determine ASLC/AWLC/PDW values and thereby coefficients and predictions.

Cross-validation setup and data independence: lack of specification about whether CV was stratified by class or by document source, and whether documents from the same source appear in both train/test folds, creates ambiguous risk of optimistic performance estimates.

Uncertainty quantification absent: no standard errors or confidence intervals are provided for Fleiss' kappa, pairwise correlations, regression coefficients, or accuracy estimates; fold-wise variability is reported only as per-fold numbers without aggregate dispersion measures.

Prediction-to-class mapping: the decision to round continuous regression outputs to the nearest integer for classification is a heuristic; its comparative performance versus ordinal regression or multiclass classifiers is untested, leaving model calibration and borderline-case behavior uncertain.

Distributional representativeness: sources/domains of collected documents are described at a high level but per-source counts and their alignment with target application domains are not provided, leaving generalizability to different registers unclear.
model_diversity_effects: Structure-focused reviewers emphasized logical consistency and identified places where reasoning chains depend on underspecified procedures (exposes PDW2 leakage, rounding decision, and feature-selection heuristic).

Methodology/auditing reviewers prioritized reproducibility and validity checks: per-fold PDW2 derivation, preprocessing scripts, fold construction, and statistical uncertainty estimates were demanded as necessary to validate claims.

Incremental novelty assessors highlighted the resource (corpus) as the main contribution and requested evidence that the empirical novelty (PDW2 advantage) is not an artifact; they were comparatively sympathetic to modest modeling choices if reproducibility is established.

Disruptive/creative lens reviewers treated the corpus + PDW2 idea as an innovation signal but conditioned their positive stance on fixing leakage and transparency issues; they urged experimental robustness (per-fold recomputation, external validation) before treating the PDW2 result as broadly generalizable.
Claim-verification reviewers focused on evidence consistency and flagged missing numerical uncertainty (SEs/CIs) and absent per-document rater data as barriers to independent verification.
meta_review.editor_guidance: Priority actions for verification and decision support: (1) Require the authors to explicitly state whether PDW2 was constructed once from the full corpus or recomputed per CV fold. If global PDW2 was used, request re-running experiments with PDW2 derived only from training folds (or an external 'easy' list) and report revised correlations and accuracies. (2) Require release of preprocessing code (tokenizer/syllabifier, normalization rules), or precise algorithmic descriptions, plus the PDW2 list and scripts to build it, to enable reproducibility and leakage checks. (3) Request full annotation metadata: per-document raw rater scores and which raters labeled which documents, and reporting of confidence intervals for Fleiss' kappa and analysis of disagreement patterns. (4) Ask for expanded evaluation artifacts: per-fold confusion matrices, per-class precision/recall/F1, class supports per fold, and statistical uncertainty (SEs/95% CIs or bootstrapped intervals) for correlations, regression coefficients, and accuracies. (5) Insist on clearer CV protocol details: stratification strategy, random seeds, and whether fold construction considered document-source grouping; if sources are clustered, recommend grouped CV. (6) Request ablations and robustness checks: (a) recompute PDW2 per-fold, (b) sensitivity to feature-selection thresholds and multicollinearity diagnostics (VIFs), (c) alternative modeling choices (ordinal regression, multinomial logistic, and at least one regularized model), and (d) baseline comparisons (majority-class, Nguyen & Henkin reimplementations, and simple ML baselines). (7) Prefer that the authors provide an external or domain-stratified held-out evaluation (or explicit limitations if not possible). These steps will resolve the main methodological uncertainties and let the editor centrally weigh reproducibility, stability, and generalizability evidence when deciding next steps.
meta_review.author_guidance: Actionable requests to strengthen the manuscript: (1) PDW2 provenance: explicitly document how PDW2 was created. If PDW2 was built using the full corpus, recompute it within each CV training split and re-run the experiments; report both sets of results (global PDW2 vs per-fold PDW2). Share the PDW2 list and the script used to build it. (2) Preprocessing reproducibility: provide exact preprocessing steps and code (or pseudocode): normalization of Unicode/diacritics, tokenizer/segmenter used, rules for syllable vs word splitting, punctuation handling, lowercasing, and any filtering. Include a small annotated example showing raw text -> tokens -> counted units. (3) Annotation transparency: release per-document rater assignments (which 3 raters, their raw scores) so Fleiss' kappa can be recomputed and disagreement patterns analyzed; provide confidence intervals for kappa and per-class agreement statistics. (4) Statistical uncertainty and diagnostics: report standard errors or 95% confidence intervals for correlations and regression coefficients (per-fold and aggregated), report VIFs for retained features, and include residual diagnostics (e.g., normality, heteroscedasticity) or bootstrap checks. (5) Cross-validation clarity: describe fold construction (stratified by class? grouped by source?), include random seeds, and provide per-fold class supports and confusion matrices. If documents from same source can leak information, consider grouped CV. (6) Modeling alternatives and ablations: compare OLS+rounding to ordinal logistic regression and multiclass classifiers; conduct sensitivity analysis for the correlation-based selection threshold (e.g., 0.7, 0.8, 0.9) and try regularized regressions (ridge/lasso) to assess coefficient stability. (7) Baselines and external tests: report simple baselines (majority class, Nguyen & Henkin formulae re-implemented on this corpus, and at least one ML baseline) and, if possible, evaluate on external or held-out domain data to quantify generalizability. (8) Release artifacts: share the corpus (or appropriate anonymized subset), PDW2, preprocessing and model code, and the exact CV splits used so independent reproduction and auditing can occur.
transparency_report: Required artifacts to enable reproducibility and auditing: (a) raw corpus with per-document metadata (source/domain labels, document IDs), (b) per-document raw rater scores and rater IDs to recompute inter-annotator agreement, (c) PDW2 (and PDW1/PDS lists) and scripts used to build them, (d) preprocessing scripts (tokenization/syllabification/normalization steps), (e) feature-extraction code, (f) model training/evaluation code including CV split definitions and random seeds, and (g) per-fold outputs: confusion matrices, per-class counts, and fold-wise coefficients.

Reporting items currently missing or underspecified: explicit statement whether PDW2 was computed globally or per training fold; algorithmic tokenizer/ syllabifier descriptions; VIFs, SEs/CIs for regression coefficients; confidence intervals for reported accuracies and correlations; and fold construction details (stratified/grouped or not).
Suggested minimal reproducibility metadata: software/tool versions, random seeds, list of sources and counts per source, and sample processed documents illustrating tokenization and syllable counts.
epistemic_limits: This synthesis is based exclusively on the provided manuscript excerpts and detailed reviewer summaries, not on raw data, code, or independent reruns. I cannot recompute Fleiss' kappa, correlations, or model fits, nor can I confirm whether PDW2 was constructed with or without access to test-fold data. Statements about leakage, coefficient stability, and generalizability are therefore inferential: they identify plausible methodological risks supported by reviewer consensus but cannot determine whether those risks were realized in the authors' experiments. Any final judgment about the formula's external validity or the true magnitude of predictive performance requires the empirical checks requested above (per-fold PDW2 recomputation, preprocessing code, uncertainty quantification, and external evaluation).

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript reports a new Vietnamese readability resource (996 documents labeled Easy/Normal/Difficult) and an interpretable linear readability formula using three corpus-derived surface features (ASLC, AWLC, PDW2). Within the authors' 5-fold cross-validation and rounding-to-class protocol the formula attains ~81% average in-corpus accuracy. Multiple reviewers agree the corpus scale and language-aware feature choices are valuable; however, important methodological and reporting gaps limit confidence in the claimed predictive validity and generalizability. The principal unresolved risks are (1) possible circularity/leakage because PDW2 (the corpus-derived "easy" word list) appears to be built from Easy documents of the same corpus, (2) underspecified preprocessing/tokenization and syllable-counting procedures that directly affect core features, (3) missing uncertainty quantification (SEs/CIs) and diagnostics for regression and annotation agreement, and (4) incomplete cross-validation details (stratification, source grouping, whether PDW2 was recomputed per fold).
strengths: Substantially larger Vietnamese readability corpus (996 documents) than prior local resources, enabling more robust empirical study.
Features are explicitly adapted to Vietnamese orthography (character- and syllable-based sentence/word length measures) and are interpretable and easy to compute.
The final model is simple and transparent (explicit coefficients for ASLC, AWLC, PDW2 and an intercept), which favors practical deployment if validated.
Empirical finding that a corpus-derived frequent-word list (PDW2) correlates strongly with the corpus labels is a potentially useful language-specific observation (innovation signal).
limitations: Potential circularity/leakage: PDW2 is described as "1,000 frequent words extracted from all easy documents of our built corpus." If PDW2 was constructed once on the full corpus rather than only from training data per CV fold, the feature may encode label-derived signals and inflate reported correlations and accuracy.

Underspecified preprocessing: tokenization, syllable segmentation, diacritic/normalization choices, and punctuation handling are described informally but no algorithmic rules or code are provided; these choices materially affect ASLC/AWLC/PDW2 values and reproducibility.

Missing statistical uncertainty and diagnostics: Fleiss' kappa, correlations, regression coefficients, and reported accuracies lack standard errors, confidence intervals, or p-values; multicollinearity diagnostics (e.g., VIFs) and residual analyses for the linear model are not reported.

Cross-validation and evaluation details incomplete: the manuscript does not state whether folds were stratified by class or grouped by source, whether PDW2 was recomputed per training fold, nor are per-fold confusion matrices and class supports provided — all of which are necessary to assess robustness and risk of optimistic estimates.
open_questions: Was PDW2 constructed once using the full corpus (including documents held out in CV) or recomputed independently within each training fold? Please provide code and the exact procedure used to build PDW2.

Provide precise preprocessing rules and implementation: which tokenizer/segmenter was used, how syllable counts were computed, how diacritics and punctuation were normalized/handled, and an example mapping raw text → tokenized/syllabified output.

Please report uncertainty measures: 95% confidence intervals (or SEs) for Fleiss' kappa, feature–label correlations, regression coefficients (per-fold and aggregated), and accuracy estimates (e.g., bootstrap CIs), and VIFs for retained predictors.

Describe CV fold construction: were folds stratified by label and/or source? Were documents from the same source allowed in both train and test folds? Provide per-fold confusion matrices and class support counts.

Have alternative modeling decisions been tried and compared (ordinal logistic regression, multiclass classifiers, or regression without rounding)? If so, report comparative results and calibration/per-class metrics.
If external test data are unavailable, can the authors perform domain-holdout experiments (withhold entire source types) to approximate generalizability and report performance drops, if any?
consensus_snapshot: Reviewers concur that the corpus scale and language-aware feature engineering are valuable contributions for Vietnamese readability research.

All reviewers identify PDW2 (corpus-derived frequent-word list) as a key predictor with strong in-corpus correlation, but they uniformly flag the potential for leakage unless PDW2 was computed strictly from training data per fold.
There is agreement that reproducibility artifacts are missing: explicit preprocessing code, PDW2 construction scripts/lists, per-document rater assignments, and CV split definitions.

The analytic pipeline (feature correlation → correlation-threshold selection → linear regression with 5-fold CV → rounding) is coherent, but the methodological choices (threshold 0.9, averaging coefficients, rounding) require ablation and justification.
disagreement_snapshot: Some reviewers view Fleiss' kappa = 0.422 as moderate but acceptable given task subjectivity and corpus scale; others treat it as substantive label noise requiring deeper per-rater analysis before trusting model accuracy.

Assessments of novelty vary: several reviewers treat the work as meaningful primarily because of dataset scale (incremental methodological novelty), while others see the PDW2 result as a stronger innovation signal conditional on eliminating leakage.

Severity assigned to lack of external validation differs: a subset views absence of out-of-domain testing as a major limitation that undermines practical claims, while others consider it an important but addressable next step that does not negate in-corpus findings.
uncertainty_snapshot: High uncertainty about whether PDW2 construction leaked label information into features; confirmed provenance is required to judge reported accuracy.
Uncertainty in measured feature values due to underspecified tokenization/syllable counting; replication could yield materially different ASLC/AWLC/PDW2 and thus coefficients.
Unquantified variability: fold-wise differences exist but without SEs/CIs it is unclear whether coefficients and accuracies are stable or sensitive to splits.
Unknown generalizability: performance on other Vietnamese domains/registers or on finer-grained readability levels is untested and therefore uncertain.
source_trace: Manuscript Table 1 and Section 3.1: corpus counts (Easy 235, Normal 413, Difficult 348; Overall 996) and annotation protocol (10 experts, 3 raters per doc).
Manuscript Table 2 and Section 3.3: pairwise correlations showing TR vs PDW2 = 0.786, TR vs AWLC = 0.774, TR vs ASLC = 0.695, and PDW1/PDS1 correlations near 0.103/0.051.

Manuscript Equation 16 and Table 3: final averaged coefficients Readability = 0.004*ASLC + 0.1905*AWLC + 2.7147*PDW2 − 0.7295 and per-fold coefficient/accuracy listings (fold-averaged overall accuracy ≈ 0.8102).
Manuscript Section 3.2: description that PDW2 = "1,000 frequent words extracted from all easy documents of our built corpus" (source of circularity concern).

Shared analysis and specialist reviews: repeated requests for PDW2 per-fold recomputation, preprocessing code, per-document rater assignments, VIFs/SEs, and external/holdout evaluation; these form the basis for the methodological concerns listed above.
transparency_notes: Key transparency items currently missing or underspecified: (1) exact PDW2 construction script and the PDW2 word list(s); (2) preprocessing code for tokenization, syllable segmentation, diacritic normalization, and punctuation handling; (3) per-document rater assignments (which 3 of 10 rated each document and their raw scores) to recompute Fleiss' kappa and analyze disagreements; (4) CV split definitions including stratification/grouping criteria and random seeds; (5) per-fold confusion matrices, class supports, coefficient SEs/CIs and VIFs; (6) scripts to reproduce feature extraction, model fitting, and evaluation. Providing these artifacts (or detailed algorithmic descriptions where sharing data is restricted) is essential to test leakage, reproduce counts, and validate reported metrics.
human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: Request targeted revisions and verification steps before concluding on the formula's validity: (1) Require authors to state explicitly whether PDW2 was constructed globally or per-training-fold. If global, request re-running CV with PDW2 derived only from training data per fold and report updated results. (2) Insist on release (or detailed description) of preprocessing/tokenization/syllabification code and PDW2 list and scripts to build it. (3) Require full annotation metadata (per-document rater IDs and scores) and confidence intervals for Fleiss' kappa; ask for analysis of disagreement patterns. (4) Ask for per-fold confusion matrices, per-class precision/recall/F1, fold-wise coefficient SEs/CIs, and VIFs for retained predictors. (5) Request ablations: sensitivity to the 0.9 correlation threshold, regularized models (ridge/lasso), and alternative mapping methods (ordinal logistic or multiclass classifiers) to assess robustness of the OLS+rounding choice. (6) Prefer demonstration of external or domain-holdout evaluation (or, if unavailable, a domain-stratified CV) to assess generalizability. These checks address the primary epistemic risks (leakage, preprocessing ambiguity, and uncertainty quantification) flagged by reviewers.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: Actionable recommendations to strengthen claims and reproducibility: (1) Clarify PDW2 provenance; if PDW2 was computed on the full corpus, recompute PDW2 per training fold and re-run CV, then report both original and corrected results and the PDW2 lists used. (2) Publish preprocessing and feature-extraction code (tokenizer/segmenter, syllable-count algorithm, normalization rules) or detailed pseudocode plus small processed examples. (3) Release per-document annotation data (rater IDs and raw scores) so kappa and per-document disagreement can be independently assessed; report kappa CIs and per-class agreement. (4) Provide uncertainty quantification: SEs/CIs for correlations, regression coefficients (per-fold and aggregate), and accuracy estimates (bootstrap or analytic CIs); report VIFs and residual diagnostics. (5) Document CV splitting strategy (stratification/grouping, random seed) and provide per-fold confusion matrices and class supports. (6) Run ablation and robustness checks: (a) sensitivity of feature selection threshold, (b) regularized regressions to check coefficient stability, (c) ordinal logistic/multiclass classifiers in addition to OLS+rounding, and (d) baseline comparisons (majority-class, reimplemented Nguyen & Henkin formula, simple ML classifier). (7) If possible, evaluate on external or domain-holdout data to demonstrate generalizability; if not possible, explicitly state limitations and caution against overgeneralization. (8) Share PDW2 and other derived lists and the exact CV splits to enable independent replication.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
The paper provides a substantially larger Vietnamese readability corpus (996 documents) and an interpretable linear readability formula built from Vietnamese-aware surface features (average sentence length in characters ASLC, average word length in characters AWLC, and percent difficult words PDW2 derived from a corpus 'easy' list). Reported in-corpus performance under the authors' 5-fold CV plus rounding-to-class protocol is ≈81% overall accuracy. The resource scale and language-specific feature engineering are meaningful contributions for Vietnamese readability research.

Strengths:
- Corpus size: nearly 1,000 labeled documents (much larger than prior Vietnamese datasets).  
- Language-aware, interpretable features and a simple linear formula facilitating practical use.  
- PDW2 shows strong in-corpus correlation suggesting corpus-derived frequent-word lists may capture lexical difficulty signals for Vietnamese.

Limitations:
- PDW2 circularity risk: PDW2 was described as built from all Easy documents of the corpus. If PDW2 was computed globally rather than only from training data within each CV fold, feature leakage could inflate correlations and predictive performance.  
- Reproducibility gap: preprocessing (tokenization, syllable counting, diacritic/punctuation handling) is underspecified and no code or pseudocode is provided; these choices directly affect ASLC/AWLC/PDW2 and thus coefficients.  
- Statistical uncertainty missing: no SEs/CIs reported for Fleiss' kappa, correlations, regression coefficients, or accuracy estimates; no VIFs or residual diagnostics provided.  
- CV and evaluation details incomplete: fold stratification/grouping by source is not stated; per-fold confusion matrices and class supports are not shown, limiting assessment of robustness and class-wise behavior.

Open Questions:
1) Was PDW2 built globally or per-training-fold? Please provide the script and the PDW2 list(s) and, if necessary, rerun CV with per-fold PDW2 and report updated metrics.  
2) Provide exact preprocessing pipeline (tokenizer/segmenter, syllable-count algorithm, normalization) and an example showing raw text → tokenized/syllabified output → computed feature values.  
3) Report uncertainty estimates: 95% CIs or SEs for Fleiss' kappa, feature–label correlations, regression coefficients (per-fold and aggregated), and accuracy (e.g., via bootstrap); include VIFs and residual diagnostics.  
4) Clarify CV protocol: were folds stratified by class and/or grouped by document source? Provide per-fold confusion matrices, class supports, and random seeds.  
5) How does OLS+rounding compare to ordinal logistic regression and multiclass classifiers (accuracy, calibration, per-class precision/recall)?
